cards.title: Map Google Ads campaign types to funnel stage before allocating budget
cards.summary: Six Google Ads campaign types (Search, Shopping, Display, Demand Gen, Video, PMax) each sit at a different funnel stage and should be launched in a specific order.
cards.use_when: Deciding which Google Ads campaign types to launch first when moving budget over from Meta or building a new Google account for a DTC store.
steps: Recognise the six types: Search (keyword text ads, top/bottom of SERP), Shopping (product feed cards with image, price, ratings, delivery), Display (image banners across ~3M sites/apps, strongest for remarketing), Demand Gen (image+video across YouTube Shorts, Discover, Gmail; targets interests/life events/in-market rather than active search), Video/YouTube (Shorts, 6-second bumpers, skippable in-stream after 5s, non-skippable in-stream, in-feed), and Performance Max (all of the above in one campaign).
Launch in the source's recommended chronological order: Search and Shopping first (bottom/mid funnel), then remarketing and PMax (mid funnel), then Demand Gen last to scale top-funnel demand.
Treat Search and Shopping as the non-negotiable core — the source argues you will not succeed on Google Ads without nailing these two, and everything else is a bonus.
Do not spread budget thin across all six types before Search and Shopping are working; layer on the rest once you see success.
For each type you run, decide whether it is branded or non-branded (Search and Shopping are both split this way) since the economics and purposes differ.
caveats: PMax is easy to set up but hard to diagnose because it blends all placements — the source does not recommend it for most beginners for exactly that reason.
The timing of 'then add PMax and Demand Gen' is not quantified; success of Search/Shopping is the gate, not a fixed date.

cards.title: Split branded and non-branded Search/Shopping to protect and grow
cards.summary: Branded campaigns defend traffic and cheaply feed the algorithm; non-branded campaigns are where new-customer growth actually happens.
cards.use_when: Structuring Search and Shopping campaigns for a store, particularly when deciding how much budget to put behind the brand name versus generic product queries.
steps: Run branded Search/Shopping campaigns bidding on your own brand name (e.g. 'Nike' or 'Nike running shoes') to defend against competitors bidding on your brand and capturing traffic already looking for you.

Run non-branded Search/Shopping campaigns on generic product queries (e.g. 'women's running shoes') as the main new-customer growth lever — this is where a Nike-style brand still shows up to convert shoppers comparing Brooks, Lululemon and Adidas.

Use low-budget, high-ROAS branded campaigns deliberately as a cheap conversion-data feed for the algorithm, improving the machine learning that then powers the more expensive non-branded, new-customer campaigns.
Explicitly add your branded terms as exact-match negative keywords inside non-branded campaigns, so brand searches do not get absorbed into non-branded reporting and distort attribution and ROAS.
Review branded vs non-branded reporting separately — mixing them hides the true cost of acquiring new customers.
caveats: Branded ROAS is structurally high and should not be used as evidence that your non-branded acquisition is profitable.
The source notes the non-branded side is 'much more lucrative' for growth but does not supply cost or ROAS benchmarks for it.

cards.title: Use a feed-only Performance Max campaign as a feed-led retail test
cards.summary: Test a feed-led retail PMax configuration against the store baseline without assuming strict audience or channel isolation.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a feed-led versus full-asset Performance Max campaign for an ecommerce product catalog.
steps: Confirm Merchant Center linkage, eligible products, accurate prices and stock, and tested purchase-value tracking.
Treat the source feed-only approach as a test of reduced manually supplied creative. Review the actual asset-generation and URL-expansion settings in the current interface.
Monitor channel delivery, product performance and new versus returning customer outcomes; compare contribution and acquisition cost with the existing Shopping or full-asset setup.
Do not classify the campaign as remarketing-only or promise Shopping-only delivery. Use a campaign with appropriate audience controls when strict remarketing is required.
caveats: Editorial correction: PMax audience signals do not impose strict targeting; omitting manual creative does not guarantee placement isolation. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/14530785
Merchant Center data can generate assets automatically. Source examples of efficient feed-led campaigns are not delivery guarantees. https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/15865151

cards.title: Run Display remarketing against exact previously-viewed products
cards.summary: Display campaigns are strongest for remarketing, and when tagged correctly they can show shoppers the exact products they viewed or carted.
cards.use_when: Setting up retargeting for a store where shoppers browse product pages or add to cart but do not purchase.
steps: Install the tagging that records which products a user viewed and which they added to cart.
Configure Display campaigns so the creative serves the specific product the shopper interacted with, not a generic brand banner.
Keep the CTA explicit (e.g. a 'Shop Now' style button) pointing at that product or collection.
Accept that Display is less popular than it once was but can still work when the creative is genuinely product-specific rather than generic branding.
Expect Display focus on the mid-funnel: it re-engages people who already know the brand rather than creating new demand.
caveats: Display reach spans roughly 3 million sites and apps, so placement quality varies; generic banners without product specificity are the setup the source warns against relying on.
The source gives no Display performance benchmarks here beyond noting Display CTRs run lower than Search and Shopping.

cards.title: Use Demand Gen to create demand on YouTube Shorts, Discover and Gmail
cards.summary: Demand Gen blends image and video ads across YouTube Shorts, the Discover feed and Gmail promotions to reach people who are not actively searching yet.
cards.use_when: Planning top-funnel paid acquisition to reach cold or in-market audiences on Google's non-search surfaces, or looking for a cheaper video placement than Instagram Reels.
steps: Set up Demand Gen campaigns to serve image and video ads across YouTube (including Shorts), the Discover feed on mobile Chrome below the search box, and the promotions tab in Gmail.
Target either cold audiences based on interests, life events, or in-market signals, or remarket to people who previously interacted with your store.
Consider YouTube Shorts specifically for ecommerce — the source observes competition there is less fierce than on Instagram Reels and the cost to serve tends to be lower.
Treat Demand Gen as demand creation rather than demand capture; it reaches people who are not yet searching for your products.
Keep it last in the launch sequence — after Search and Shopping are proven — since the source positions it as top-funnel scaling.
caveats: Placement cost observations are the source's current experience, not a guaranteed or stable benchmark; verify actual CPMs in your account.
No conversion-rate or ROAS benchmarks for Demand Gen are given in this material.

cards.title: Match YouTube ad format to the job the video needs to do
cards.summary: YouTube offers Shorts, bumper, skippable in-stream, non-skippable in-stream and in-feed formats, each with different length, skip rules and placements.
cards.use_when: Choosing which YouTube video ad format to produce and buy for a store's awareness, consideration or retargeting objective.
steps: Shorts — vertical, mobile-first content similar to Reels; useful for cheaper reach given lighter competition.
Bumper ads — roughly 6 seconds long and usually served at the start of a video; use for a single sharp message.
Skippable in-stream — viewer can skip after 5 seconds; served before, during or after videos.
Non-skippable in-stream — the viewer must watch the full (typically 30-second) ad; higher friction, so use sparingly.
In-feed ads — served inside YouTube's feed, including the Discover page or the suggested 'watch next' list on the right-hand side.
Pick format based on whether you need cheap reach, forced message delivery, or click-driven traffic, then produce creative to the length and aspect ratio that format requires.
caveats: The source notes YouTube ads are 'really, really effective when done right' but does not provide performance benchmarks by format.
Skips, length limits and available formats are platform-controlled and change — verify current specifications in Google Ads.

cards.title: Set the core Google Ads columns and read them in the right order
cards.summary: A consistent column set — impressions, clicks, CTR, cost, conv. value/cost, CPA, conversions, avg CPC, conversion rate — makes campaign health readable at a glance.
cards.use_when: Configuring the Google Ads campaign view so you can judge performance daily without digging through reports.
steps: Include at minimum: impressions (how many times the ad was seen), clicks, CTR (clicks ÷ impressions), cost, conversion value ÷ cost (ROAS), cost per conversion/CPA, total conversions and conversion value, average CPC, and conversion rate.
Arrange columns in the same logical order every time so you can scan any account the same way.
Read conversion value ÷ cost as the ROAS figure — dollars returned in purchase value per dollar spent.
Read conversion rate as the share of clickers who completed your chosen action (usually purchase for ecommerce).
Set a date filter deliberately — 1 day, 1 week, 30 or 60 days — and remember the numbers shift with the window.
caveats: The source's sample account shows conversion rates ranging from 14% down to 0.73% across campaigns, illustrating how misleading a single blended rate can be.
Google Ads columns are customisable and the interface changes — verify current column names.

cards.title: Judge CTR only against its campaign type, not one universal benchmark
cards.summary: Acceptable click-through rate varies enormously by campaign type, so use the source's loose ranges only as directional checks.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Search or Shopping ad copy and targeting, or diagnosing whether a campaign's click-through is genuinely weak.
steps: The source's directional expectations: non-branded Search should aim for at least 7–8% CTR; Shopping around 1%; Display typically lower still; branded Search is naturally very high.
Do not judge a campaign on CTR in isolation — treat it as a trend metric, especially for Search campaigns, and look at movement over time rather than a single snapshot.
If non-branded Search CTR sits well below the range, the likely levers are keyword-to-ad relevance, ad copy strength, offer clarity or urgency, and query match.
For Shopping, remember the click competes with rich product cards (image, price, ratings, delivery) rather than a text ad, which is why 1%-style CTRs are normal.
Avoid applying the Search target to Shopping or Display — a ~1% shopping CTR is not automatically a failure.
caveats: The source explicitly says there is no set benchmark and these are general figures, not contractual targets.
CTR is one diagnostic among many; a low CTR with strong conversion rate and ROAS may still be fine.

cards.title: Understand conversion lag with conversions vs conversions-by-conversion-time
cards.summary: Google credits conversions to the ad-click date by default, while 'by conversion time' reports the date the purchase actually happened — the gap is conversion lag.
cards.use_when: Reading weekly or recent Google Ads performance for any store with a non-impulsive consideration phase, before deciding a campaign is failing.
steps: Know the two column pairs: conversions / conversion value (credited by ad-interaction date) versus conversions by conversion time / conversion value by conversion time (credited by purchase date).
Worked example: a shopper clicks a Search ad on 1 July but buys on 4 July for $40 — the 1 July row shows 1 conversion and $40, while the 4 July row shows 0 conversions/$0 for those same columns.
In that same example, the by-conversion-time row shows 0 on 1 July and 1 conversion with $40 value on 4 July.
If your sales cycle runs long — say a 14–21 day consideration phase — the discrepancy becomes far more pronounced than in a one-week view where both dates fall inside the window.
Do not judge recent campaigns on click-dated conversions alone; revisit the same period two to three weeks later when the purchases have populated.
caveats: Attribution questions (organic/Facebook influence on the later purchase) are deliberately set aside in the source and are not resolved by these columns.
During any partial look-back window, recency-biased numbers will always look worse than the settled data.

cards.title: Read impression share to find out whether budget or ad rank is capping you
cards.summary: Search impression share splits what you missed into lost-to-rank and lost-to-budget, telling you which lever to pull.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to raise budget or improve ad quality when a Search campaign is not serving as often as it could.
steps: Read search impression share as the percentage of eligible auctions where your ad actually served (e.g. 88.75% served means 11.25% lost).
Read search absolute top impression share as the share of time you were the very first ad (position 1 only); search top impression share as positions 1–4, above organic results.
Use the delta between the two: 88.75% serving, 87.3% in positions 1–4 and 81.57% in position 1 means roughly 6% of impressions were served in positions 2–4.
Check search lost IS (rank) and search lost IS (budget) — the two must sum to your total missed impression share (e.g. 10% rank + ~1% budget = 11.25%).

If you are losing on both, fix ad rank first: it is the more efficient route because improving relevance makes the same budget go further, whereas simply raising budget leaves the inefficiency in place.

Only after maximising quality score should you bid more — raise manual CPC bids directly, or for automated strategies loosen the constraint, e.g. move a 400% tROAS target down to 350% or 300% to let Google bid more aggressively.
caveats: Loosening a tROAS target increases CPC and ad rank but directly reduces the return target — this affects margin, so treat it as a deliberate trade.
Impression-share metrics apply to Search-type campaigns; the source does not present them as universal.

cards.title: Diagnose ad rank through quality score's three components
cards.summary: Quality score (out of 10) is driven by expected CTR, landing page experience and ad relevance — improve those before paying more per click.
cards.use_when: Improving an underperforming Search campaign that is losing impression share to rank, rather than simply increasing bids.
steps: Look at quality score at keyword level and its three components — expected CTR, landing page experience and ad relevance — each rated above average, average or below average.
Expected CTR: how likely Google thinks your ad is to be clicked relative to competing ads in the auction — influenced by offer, positioning and urgency in the copy.
Landing page experience: speed, general UX, relevance of the page to both the keyword and the ad, and low bounce / high on-site engagement.
Ad relevance: how tightly the keyword and ad copy match each other and the user's query.
Work all three dimensions before touching bids; if they are maxed out, the only remaining lever for ad rank is paying a higher CPC.
Treat the ad rank formula as having exactly two inputs — relevance (which Google rewards) and bid (which Google also rewards) — and prioritise the rewarded relevance route to protect margins.
caveats: Quality score is Google's own representation and diagnostic aid, not a perfect measure; the source treats it as guidance for where to look.
Component ratings are relative (above/average/below), not absolute numbers.

cards.title: Use video metrics: impressions vs views, view rate, CPV and frequency
cards.summary: Video campaigns report views, view rate, average CPV, CPM, video-played-to percentages, watch time and impression frequency — with 'view' defined differently per format.
cards.use_when: Evaluating YouTube or video campaign creative performance and deciding whether the hook or the targeting is at fault.
steps: Distinguish an impression (the ad was seen) from a view (a higher-engagement threshold that varies by campaign type) — for some formats a view needs 30 seconds of watch time, and for videos shorter than 30 seconds it requires watching to completion.
Read the standard metrics per format: in-stream view rate of 28% versus in-feed 19% in the source's example means in-stream viewers engaged at a higher rate.
Use video-played-to-time (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) to see where in the video viewers drop off — a steep fall before 25% points at the hook, a fall later points at the body or CTA.
Check total watch time and average watch time per impression (in seconds) for how long people actually stayed.
Check average CPV, average CPM, average CPC, cost, CTR, conversions, conversion value, ROAS and conversion rate at ad group or ad level.
Check average impression frequency per user (e.g. 1.5×) over your time window to avoid over-serving the same people.
caveats: There is no single umbrella definition of a 'view' — it depends entirely on campaign type, so do not compare view rates across formats naively.
The source notes video metrics are less critical for people just starting out on Google Ads.

cards.title: Build custom columns for ROAS-by-time, device splits and average daily spend
cards.summary: Custom columns let you surface a specific formula — most usefully conversion-value-by-conversion-time ÷ cost — directly in the campaign view.
cards.use_when: Reporting on Google Ads for a store with a long consideration phase, or comparing mobile vs desktop performance at a glance.
steps: Open Modify Columns and choose '+ Custom Column'; give it a name, description and a formula.
For ROAS by time, use conversion value by conversion time ÷ cost — the same formula as ordinary ROAS but on the conversion-time value, so recent weeks fill in correctly as purchases land.
For device splits, add custom columns for mobile conversion rate vs desktop conversion rate, and mobile ROAS vs desktop ROAS, using the corresponding device-segmented metrics.
For convenience, add an average spend-per-day column so a 7-day total doesn't require mental division and you can read spend trend at a glance.
Apply these especially when you are deliberately targeting one device more aggressively than another, so the skew is visible on entry to the account.
Treat custom columns as decision-support: the goal is to have the KPIs you care about visible the moment you log in, rather than buried in reports.
caveats: The source flags custom columns as probably a step too far for complete beginners — start with the standard column set first.
Formula syntax and available metrics shift with the Google Ads interface; verify the current metric names.

cards.title: Link GA4 to Google Ads via Admin → Product links, then demote the imported purchase action
cards.summary: Connecting GA4 and Google Ads enables importing GA4 audiences and conversion actions — but the imported purchase action must be set to secondary to avoid double counting.
cards.use_when: Setting up GA4-to-Google-Ads reporting and audience imports for a Shopify store, or auditing an account whose ROAS suddenly doubled after linking analytics.
steps: In GA4, go to Admin → Property settings → Product links → Google Ads links.
Enter your Google Ads account ID (the purely numeric ID in the Google Ads top toolbar) into the search field and click Link.
On the Link screen, decide on settings such as personalised advertising and auto-tagging, confirm the ad account number and name, and click Submit.
After linking, go to Conversion actions in Google Ads and check what has been imported — typically a GA4 purchase action appears.

If you already have a purchase conversion action (from Google Tag Manager, a third-party tool, or the Google and YouTube app connecting Shopify to Google Ads), the imported GA4 purchase action will by default be primary and will affect bidding and reporting alongside the existing one.

The consequence of running two primary purchase actions is double counting: ROAS and purchases can appear to double almost overnight. Change the GA4-imported purchase action to secondary so it still fires for observation and as a fallback if the primary breaks, but does not double count.
Never use the GA4-imported action as your primary — the source's agency always uses an alternative method as primary.
caveats: This is a Shopify/ecommerce-oriented setup; the linking path and option names may change in the GA4 and Google Ads interfaces.
The double-count spike can look like a performance win — treat a sudden ROAS doubling after a GA4 link as a red flag, not a victory.

cards.title: Use four GA4 reports to sanity-check paid traffic quality
cards.summary: User attributes, monetization purchases, landing pages and channel reports give an ecommerce operator a quick outside-view of what paid traffic is doing on site.
cards.use_when: Reviewing store traffic quality every couple of weeks, especially to see how paid landing pages and channels are performing beyond Google Ads' own numbers.
steps: User attributes: break users down by country, city, gender, age, language and Google-tagged interests to sanity-check who the typical customer is.
Monetization → e-commerce purchases: see how often each product was viewed, added to cart and purchased, plus the revenue per product — all in one place.

Landing pages report: review sessions, active users, new users and average engagement time per session, then dig into bounce rates — this is where the source says GA4 is genuinely powerful for spotting weak paid-traffic landing pages.
Channels report: view first-user and primary channel groupings (direct, organic search, cross-network, paid search, organic shopping, etc.) and drill into source and medium.
Make sure UTM parameters are flowing through from all paid media so channel and source/medium attribution is actually usable.
Understand that most of this is also available in your CMS (e.g. Shopify) — use GA4 for the consolidated view rather than as the only source.
caveats: The source notes many ecommerce brand owners dislike GA4 and use alternate platforms — using it is optional, not mandatory.
GA4 is free and useful but requires familiarisation with its navigation; the four reports here are a starting shortlist, not the full surface.

cards.title: Build a 30-day cart-abandoner audience in GA4 and import it to Google Ads
cards.summary: Include users who triggered add-to-cart in the last 30 days and exclude purchasers, then import the audience for specific cart-recovery remarketing.
cards.use_when: Setting up cart-abandonment retargeting for a store, or creating a high-intent audience for Google Ads remarketing campaigns.
steps: In GA4 go to Admin → Data display → Audiences and create a new audience.
Set the include condition to 'add to cart' (a pre-built GA4 event) with a 30-day membership duration.
Add an exclusion condition: exclude users who have purchased — otherwise you will re-target people who already converted and waste spend.
The source's example: 4.2K add-to-cart users over 30 days (15% of total users); excluding 603 purchasers left ~3.6K genuine cart abandoners — a sizeable audience.
Mark the audience as a key audience so it can be imported into Google Ads.

In Google Ads remarketing, use the specificity this audience allows — e.g. 'saw you weren't ready to make a purchase, here's a discount code or free shipping' — rather than generic site-visitor messaging.
Optionally create a separate post-purchase audience to serve upsell messaging in the immediate post-purchase window, rather than mixing them into the cart-abandoner set.
caveats: Audience sizes like 4.2K/3.6K are from the source's account and will differ entirely for your store.
The audience quality depends on add-to-cart events being correctly tracked in GA4; bad event data makes the exclusion logic meaningless.

cards.title: Fix conversion tracking before anything else — it feeds you and the algorithm
cards.summary: Without correct conversion tracking both you and Google's automated bidding are blind, making every other optimisation moot.
cards.use_when: Starting Google Ads for a store, or auditing an account that is running automated bid strategies on unreliable conversion data.
steps: Accept the source's framing: conversion tracking tells you whether a click led to a purchase, and it gives Google's automated bid strategies the positive and negative feedback they learn from — without it you may as well be lighting ad spend on fire.
For a Shopify store, install the Google and YouTube app in Sales channels and connect it using a single master Google account linked to all your Google properties (Ads, Merchant Center, Analytics).
Select your Google Ads account in the app's dropdown — this automatically imports Shopify's API conversion actions, turns conversion measurement on, and is the 80–90%-of-the-way-there quick route.
Check that enhanced conversions are enabled and the Google tag is firing.

If you are serious about Google Ads, go further and implement fully in Google Tag Manager, because more conversion data fed to the algorithm means better performance — the source's agency uses a dedicated pixel (Feed Army) for enhanced tracking and remarketing.
Audit regularly for the common tracking failures the source calls cardinal sins — missing or duplicated conversion actions are the ones that quietly wreck automated bidding.
caveats: The simple Shopify app route is presented as reaching 80–90% of a full implementation, not as a complete solution.
Tool names, app flow and toggle labels (enhanced conversions, Google tag) change over time — verify the current setup in the relevant interfaces.

cards.title: Consolidate everything under one master Google account
cards.summary: Using a single Google account linked to Ads, Merchant Center and Analytics prevents broken connections and duplicated setup.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning up a store's Google ecosystem before connecting Shopify, Merchant Center feeds or GA4.
steps: Create or choose one master Google account that owns or manages your Google Ads account.
Sign in to the Google and YouTube app (or equivalent connection tool) with that master account so the Google Ads account appears in the dropdown by name or number.
Link the same master account to Google Merchant Center (the product feed that powers Shopping and PMax) and to GA4.
Select the correct Google Ads account in each connection so conversion actions import to the right place.
Avoid splitting ownership across multiple Google logins — it is the root of connection failures and duplicated conversion actions.
caveats: The source presents this as ideal setup hygiene rather than a strictly enforced requirement; the important outcome is that Ads, Merchant Center and Analytics all talk to each other.
Google account and linking interfaces change — verify current steps.

cards.title: Adopt Google Ads as the stability layer under Meta-led acquisition
cards.summary: The source's positioning is that Google Ads should be the reliable, always-on acquisition backbone for DTC brands rather than the flashiest channel.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and why to diversify a Meta-dependent store into Google, and how to frame the channel's role internally.
steps: Diagnose Meta dependency risk: when Meta works it works, but CPM spikes, conversion drops, ad-account bans and revenue stalls all concentrate your growth in one place.
Position Google Ads as the stability layer underneath Meta — high-intent Search and Shopping capture demand, full-funnel activity runs from education through to conversion.
Prioritise fixing leaky campaign structures and wasted spend over adding more channels.
Build reliable flows of new-customer acquisition through high-intent Search rather than chasing top-funnel volume first.
Sequence channel expansion deliberately: Search and Shopping as the backbone, then remarketing/PMax, then Demand Gen last.
caveats: This is the source's strategic opinion, framed from an agency that has worked with 80+ DTC brands and $50M+ in new-customer revenue — it is a thesis, not a benchmarked guarantee.
Google Ads being 'more reliable' than Meta is a claim about volatility, not about absolute performance ceilings.

cards.title: Threshold the switch from Maximize Clicks to value-based bidding
cards.summary: Move bidding from Maximize Clicks (data gathering) to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS once you reach 15–30 conversions per month.
cards.use_when: Choosing a bid strategy for a new or low-volume Google Ads campaign, and deciding when to graduate to automated value bidding.
steps: Start new campaigns on Maximize Clicks while gathering initial data — the goal at this stage is volume of signal, not efficiency.
Once the campaign reaches roughly 15–30 conversions per month, switch to Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS so the algorithm optimises toward value rather than clicks.
Before switching, make sure conversion tracking is accurate — value bidding on broken or duplicated conversion data will optimise in the wrong direction.
After switching, monitor impression share lost to rank and budget, and adjust the tROAS target (e.g. loosening 400% to 350% or 300%) if you need Google to bid more aggressively.
Treat the 15–30 figure as the source's starting threshold for having enough conversions for value-based learning, not a hard calculation.
caveats: Below the threshold, value-based bidding typically lacks enough signal to be effective — the source's band is a heuristic.
Changing bid strategy resets learning, so make the transition deliberately rather than flipping back and forth.

editorial_review: Removed routing-only material and corrected feed-only PMax audience/placement assumptions.
